calm.t: #recent#, several households below town found that their well water had begun to taste wrong. This paper has made some inquiries.
#weather#, the well water downriver began to taste chalky, and the families along that stretch have talked of little else since.
Families downriver say that lately they let a bucket from the well stand half a day before they dare to drink from it.
#season_open#, several households below town have grown wary of drinking from their own wells.
Among the goods the sawmill ordered through the post office this season, one came in a quantity that is hard to account for.

neutral.t: The wells downriver have tasted wrong for some time now. This paper's inquiries suggest the matter may be connected with the sawmill upstream, owned by {culprit}.
#recent#, families downriver said their well water was not right. Followed upstream, the trouble led to the sawmill.
#weather#, several households downriver no longer trust their own wells. The first thing upstream of them is the sawmill owned by {culprit.full}.

neutral: The river runs past the sawmill's gate, and below it lie the wells of several households.

neutral.t: A few households along the river have been worried about their wells lately.

neutral: This paper has spent several weeks following a matter between the sawmill and the families downriver.

hot.t: Families downriver have been drinking bitter water for weeks, and no one has told them why. This paper will: the trouble starts at the sawmill owned by {culprit}.
Someone has been pouring something into the river, and the children downriver drink from that river every day.
What are the children downriver drinking? {culprit.full} ought to come and taste it.

scene.t: The few households downriver draw their drinking water from their own wells, and none of those wells stands more than a few dozen paces from the river.
In summer the river runs low, and the children downriver spend their afternoons picking stones off the gravel bars.

smell.note: {victim}'s well water has tasted of lime for several weeks
prose: {victim}'s well water has tasted of lime these several weeks, and boiling does not take it out.
At the home of {victim}, downriver, the well water has tasted chalky for several weeks.
the water in {victim}'s well has gone bad, and {victim.ta} says it has been that way for weeks.

lime.note: {culprit} ordered forty sacks of lime through the post office, more than the sawmill could ever use
prose: {culprit} ordered forty sacks of lime by mail this month, far more than the sawmill ordinarily uses.
{culprit} placed a single order for forty sacks of lime. Lime is commonly used to cover the smell of waste.
the sawmill took delivery of forty sacks of lime in one order, and the order was placed by {culprit}.

prose.t: !This paper looked at the order slips at the post office: {culprit} ordered forty sacks of lime this month. The sawmill does not ordinarily use that much in a year.

dump.note: {culprit} had men pour the mill's waste into the river under cover of night
prose: men working for {culprit} carried the mill's waste down to #river# #night# and emptied it, barrel after barrel.
#night#, men wheeled barrels from the back gate of the sawmill to the water's edge and tipped them into the river. They were acting on the orders of {culprit}.

prose.t: the mill's waste went into the river under cover of darkness, and {culprit} knew of it.
!#night#, this paper's reporter kept watch on the riverbank and saw several barrels wheeled out of the sawmill's back gate and emptied into the river.
!#night#, this paper's reporter waited a long while by the river, until men from the sawmill came out with barrels and tipped them into the water, one after another.
!This paper's reporter saw it #night#: barrels came out of the sawmill's back gate and were wheeled all the way down to the bank, and what was in them went into the river.

rumor.note: {culprit} slipped money to the state inspector
prose: {culprit} has been slipping money to the state inspector.
{culprit} paid off the state inspector long ago.

detail.t: A rut runs from the back gate of the sawmill to the water's edge, worn by the wheels of a loaded barrow.
The talk in town is that some of the households downriver now carry water from the public well on the east side rather than drink their own.

calm.t: The sawmill keeps some forty families in this town in work, and that is a fact. The well water downriver is a fact as well.
Well water can go bad for any number of reasons. This paper notes only that every well that has gone bad lies below the sawmill.

neutral.t: A sawmill ordering lime is nothing strange. Forty sacks is. The mill's work cannot use so much, and the mill has not said where the rest went.
The wells are downstream, and the waste went into the river upstream. Set side by side, the two leave this paper no third explanation.

neutral: The sawmill is the largest employer in town, and the largest advertiser in this paper. This paper printed the story anyway, because the families downriver take this paper too.

hot.t: Had it been clean water, it could have been poured out by daylight. Whoever chose the night knew why.
Everybody knows whose pocket the mill's profits go into. What goes into the river, the whole town drinks.
The children downriver have drunk bitter water for a whole season, and nobody has come to say sorry.

any.t: Forty sacks of lime were ordered, and the wells taste of lime. The figure on the order slip and the taste of the water agree, and that is why this paper prints the story.
For the dumping, this paper has given its sources above. The talk of money slipped to the state inspector this paper has not been able to confirm, and it remains a rumor.
Bad well water shows only that something is wrong with the water, not whose doing it is. This paper prints it to ask the sawmill to say what it lets into the river.
One sack of lime will whitewash a room. Forty sacks would whitewash every wall at the sawmill ten times over.
The order went through the post office, with the name, the quantity and the date written on it. That needs no witness.
The owner gave the order to dump at night, and the men who did it were paid for their work. The question belongs to the one who gave the order.

denied.t: {target.short} says the sawmill's drainage has always been done properly.
{target.short} says the lime was for whitewashing the mill and keeping off insects.
{target.short} says the wells went bad because of the dry weather.

calm.t: This paper will ask again when the wells downriver are fit to drink.

hot.t: How much longer will the river stink?

calm.t: Small trade is never easy in Greyriver, and the general store has lately had more trouble than most collecting what it is owed.

calm: Nothing worries a small trader in this town like credit that never comes back.

calm.t: #season_open#, the credit book at the general store has grown by several pages.
#recent#, the pawnshop by the railway station took in a mantel clock.

neutral.t: An account at the general store has gone unpaid for six months. It stands in the name of {debtor}.
{creditor.full} has a debt on the books that will not be collected, and it has been weighing on the store.
At the general store kept by {creditor.full}, an account has stood open for six months and has still not been settled.
Trade in this town lives on credit, and dreads it too. This paper looked into one account that has stood open a long time.
#recent#, the mantel clock from the home of {debtor.full} turned up on the pawnshop counter.
This paper had a look through a certain credit book this week.
The general store has an old account on its books that has stood six months with no one coming to settle it.

hot.t: {debtor.full} goes about town as usual, but in the general store's book, a long column of figures stands after that name.
Some people eat well and dress well and never pay a cent of what they owe.
Six months on, {debtor.full} has not paid one cent against the account at the general store.

scene.t: Under the counter at the general store lies a credit book, and half the families in town have their names in it.
The end of the year is when the general store settles up, and the storekeeper goes from house to house with the credit book, one family at a time.

ledger.note: {debtor} has run an account at the general store for half a year without paying it
prose: {debtor} has bought on credit for six months without paying a cent of it.
the store's credit book has carried the name of {debtor} for half a year, for everything from flour to lamp oil.
{debtor} owes {creditor}, and the first entry was made six months ago.

prose.t: !This paper went through the credit book at the general store. The page for {debtor} begins half a year back, entry after entry, and none of it has been settled.

pawn.note: {debtor} pawned the family mantel clock at a shop near the railway station
prose: {debtor} took the family mantel clock to be pawned at a shop near the railway station.
{debtor} was seen carrying a clock into the pawnshop.
the mantel clock is gone from the parlor of {debtor}, and the ticket for it is at the shop behind the station.

rumor.note: {debtor}'s debts are gambling debts, not store accounts
prose: !Some say the debts of {debtor} are really gambling debts.
!There is another story, too, that {debtor} lost the money at cards.

detail.t: It is the pawnshop's rule that redeeming a pledge always costs more than it fetched.
The most recent entry in the credit book is two pounds of salt, last week.

calm: There is no shame in owing money; everyone runs short in times like these. But the storekeeper who gives credit has a living to make too.

calm.t: When the clock goes to the pawnshop, a household's circumstances are plain to see.

neutral.t: Still buying on credit after half a year means this is no passing shortage. Every month the storekeeper waits is another month of stock paid for out of the store's own pocket.
A thing is easily pawned, but it always costs more to get back. Short of money going in, one needs still more coming out: the longer it goes on, the more it costs.

neutral: This paper does not print the matter to make anyone a laughingstock. If the general store goes under, there will be nowhere left in town to buy a pound of flour on credit.

hot.t: A poor family owes thirty cents and the storekeeper is at the door the next day. A person of standing owes for half a year, and no one says a word.
Even the clock has gone to the pawnshop. Things in that house are a good deal tighter than they look from the street.

any.t: An account left standing at the store, a clock left at the pawnshop: the two say the same thing. There has not been enough ready money in that household for some time.
As for the talk that these are gambling debts, this paper has not confirmed it; it is only hearsay. The store account is written in a book. The two are not to be added together.
The debtor is a respectable gentleman, and that is the hardest kind of account for a storekeeper to ask after.
What {target.short} says carries weight in this town. So do the figures in that account book.
Half a year without a payment, and more goods taken on credit all the while. Kept up that long, the store is no longer selling; it is lending.
The credit book is kept by the store itself, and the one who owes could dispute it. Yet in half a year, nobody has come forward to say the book is wrong.
People who pawn things mostly mean to redeem them. A clock pawned and not redeemed means the money has stayed short.

denied: {target.short} says the matter is private, between debtor and store, and no concern of a newspaper's.

denied.t: {target.short} says the account will be settled sooner or later.
{target.short} says the clock was {target.his} own, and whether to pawn it was a family matter.

calm.t: This paper will ask again when the account is paid.

calm: This is a family matter. This paper hesitated a long while before deciding to print what it found.

hot.t: {spouse.full} has a home and family, and someone there keeps supper waiting. But #night#, {spouse.he} is out on the bridge.

hot: There is a matter in this town that everyone knows about and no one will say out loud.
{lover.full} has been much talked of lately on the church steps.
Those who sit together in church do not always go home to the same house at night.

scene.t: On summer nights the heat drives people out onto the bridge for the breeze, and they seldom drift home before ten.
On winter nights the wind comes hard across the bridge, and after nine hardly anyone crosses it.
Greyriver is a small town. Everyone knows what time the lamp goes out next door.

bridge.note: {lover} and {spouse} were seen together on the bridge late at night, by several people
prose: #night#, {lover} and {spouse} walked together on the bridge, and several people saw them.
#night#, {lover} and {spouse} stood a long while on the bridge, then left one after the other.
{lover} and {spouse} have met on the bridge late at night, and not for the first time.
#night#, {lover} and {spouse} walked together on the bridge, and several people saw them. {spouse} is married.

prose.t: !#night#, this paper's reporter passed the bridge and saw {lover} and {spouse} talking under the gas lamp. They talked a long while, then left one after the other.
!#night#, this paper's reporter saw {lover} and {spouse} walk across the bridge side by side, close together, talking in low voices.
!#night#, two people stood under the lamp at the bridge. Only on coming closer did this paper's reporter make out {lover} and {spouse}. They crossed the bridge one behind the other.
!Crossing the bridge #night#, this paper's reporter came face to face with {lover} and {spouse}. Seeing someone coming, the two fell silent.

letters.note: {spouse} mails a letter to {lover} every week
prose: {spouse} sends a letter every week, and it is addressed to {lover}.
though the two live in the same small town, {spouse} writes to {lover} every week.
the letters from {spouse} to {lover} go out once a week and have never missed.

prose.t: !The post office mail book shows a letter from {spouse} to {lover} every week.

suspect.note: {wife} already suspects where {spouse} goes at night, and has cried over it more than once
prose: {wife} has grown suspicious and has wept over it more than once.
!{wife} has told friends of waking in the night to find the other side of the bed empty.
the household of {spouse} has begun to notice, and there have been hard looks at home these days.

rumor.note: {lover} was paid to come from out of town and break up the family
prose: {lover} was brought in from out of town and paid to break up the family.
{lover} came to Greyriver because someone paid for it, and the purpose was to break up that family.

detail.t: The letters are all mailed at the post office, though the one they go to lives right here in town.

calm: This is a private matter between two households, and this paper would rather not say more. But the town is small and the talk has spread, and it is better to set down plainly what was seen than to leave people guessing.

neutral.t: The two live in the same town, a few minutes' walk apart, and yet a letter goes every week. When what needs saying cannot be said face to face, that is an explanation in itself.
There is no law against a few words on a bridge at night. Keeping it from one's own family is another matter.

neutral: This paper does not judge who is right and who is wrong. Both households still live in this town, and how they go on from here is their own affair.

hot.t: The hardest part of this falls on the one who sits at home and waits.
A person with a home ought to be in it at night.

any.t: Walking together on the bridge may be chance. A letter every week is not.
Someone goes out at night; someone at home has wept more than once; and two people were seen walking together on the bridge. Set side by side, these things tell the same story.
As for the talk that {lover.short} was paid to come here, this paper has not confirmed it, and no one can say who paid. That much is idle talk.
This town has always held its schoolteachers to a stricter account than other people. That may not be fair to {target.short}.
{target.short} has taken the measurements of half the households in town. Knowing so many people means a great many tongues.
The lamp on the bridge burns all night, and anyone who passes is seen. Someone truly keeping a secret would not choose that spot; choosing it suggests they thought nobody would be about.
Of two people walking together at night, this paper can write only what was seen. What was said and where they went, this paper does not know and will not guess.
The post office knows where every letter goes, but not what is in it. So it is with this paper.
A letter a week comes to fifty-odd in a year. An ordinary acquaintance does not run to so many.
The suspicion came from within the family itself, and this paper has not asked what is suspected. The town need not guess on that family's behalf.
Someone who has wept more than once is not weeping over one late night.

denied.t: {target.short} says that on the evening in question they met purely by chance.
{target.short} says the two of them are only friends.
{target.short} says the letters are about nothing but ordinary business.

calm: This paper will write no more about it.

For some weeks now, {boss.full} has been trying to answer one question: where did the things missing from the tool room go?

#recent#, the river-bend farm put a batch of new saw blades to work. This paper looked into where they came from.

neutral: There is a matter at the sawmill the mill has not spoken of publicly. This paper has learned some of it.

neutral.t: Since things went missing at the sawmill, nobody on the crew has been easy in his mind.

The men at the mill pinch every penny, and someone has been carrying the mill's property out the gate.
The things missing from the sawmill did not walk off by themselves. Someone carried them out and sold them.

scene.t: The sawmill whistle blows at six every morning. The men come in by the back gate and draw their tools from the tool room before they start work.
Since the cold set in there has been less work at the sawmill, and less pay to go with it.
In summer the sawmill starts early, and by first light there is a line at the tool room door.

night.note: {thief} came out the back door of the sawmill at night, carrying something

!This paper's reporter saw {thief} come out of the sawmill's back door #night#, with hands far from empty.

detail.t: The tool room stands just inside the sawmill's back door, and the men draw their tools there every morning.

calm.t: A few saw blades are not worth much money. But once the men at the mill start watching each other, the work cannot get done.

neutral.t: Each time something went missing at the mill, every man there was suspected. Now at least the trail leads somewhere.
The blades went missing from the sawmill and turned up at the river-bend farm. Whose hands they passed through in between, the receipt says plainly.

neutral: This paper convicts no one. It writes down what was seen.

hot.t: Someone who comes out the back door in the middle of the night is not working late.
The mill has been asking questions for a good while. The answer was already written on the general store's receiving slips.

any.t: Leaving the mill at night with something in hand might be explained a dozen ways. But the blades then turned up on the farm's receipt, one thing after the other, and that leaves only one explanation.
Some say {boss.short} took the goods and laid the blame on a mill hand. This paper heard the story and found nothing at all to support it, so it is printed here and no more.
Everyone in town knows what an apprentice is paid.
When a mill hand loses his place, the whole town sees it. When a mill hand suddenly has money in his pocket, the town sees that too.
What went missing were saw blades and nails, not money. Whoever took them either needed them or knew who would buy them.
The receipt carries the seller's name and the date. That is more to be relied on than anything anybody saw.
There is no crime in a farm buying saw blades, and the buyer very likely did not know they were the mill's. The question is for whoever sold them.

Coming out the back door at night with something in hand: that is all this paper knows. Whether the thing belonged to the mill or to the one carrying it, this paper cannot say, and so it convicts no one here.
Work at the mill stops at dark. If people are still going in and out the back door at night, the mill should first ask who is opening it.

{target.short} says the blades sold to the farm were bought out of town.

neutral.t: How the tool room is kept from here on is for the mill to decide.

The clinic has seen only the one child, from the house of {victim.short}. But that may not be the only household that bought this syrup, and anyone who still has a bottle would do well to take it to the clinic for the doctor to look at.
It is said the syrup was made up from a doctor's prescription, but this paper has not learned which doctor. This paper does not credit it.
A stranger knocking on doors with medicine to sell: what the buyers trusted was the seal on the bottle. The seal is false, and it was the seal that took them in.

denied.t: {target.short} says the syrup was bought wholesale from a drugstore in the city, and that {target.he} does not know what is in it.
{target.short} says the seal was printed by the drugstore and has nothing to do with {target.him}.
{target.short} says nobody was made to buy.

neutral.t: Anyone with a bottle of this syrup at home may bring it to the clinic.

hot.t: Canned goods do not walk out of a freight house on their own. Somebody wheeled them out.
The cheap canned goods at the market came out of the station freight house.

scene.t: Every Tuesday the freight from the south is unloaded at the railway station, and the freight house stays open until dark.
On market day the stalls stretch from the bridge all the way to the general store door, selling a bit of everything.
Things cost more at market in winter. A can of peaches goes for ten cents.

not one of the six cases of canned peaches on the waybill can be found in the freight house, and {boss} is looking into it.

prose: {thief} has been selling canned peaches at the market at half price, five cents a can.
people at the market have bought canned peaches from {thief} at five cents a can, half what the store charges.

cart.note: {thief} wheeled a handcart with two wooden crates on it out from behind the freight house at night
prose: #night#, {thief} wheeled a handcart out from behind the freight house with two wooden crates on it.

prose.t: !#night#, behind the railway station, this paper's reporter saw {thief} wheel a handcart out of the freight house's back door, two wooden crates roped onto it.
!This paper's reporter was near the freight house that night. #night#, {thief} pushed a handcart out from behind it, the two crates so heavy that the handles kept dipping toward the ground.
!#night#, a handcart came rattling down the lane behind the freight house. This paper's reporter followed it: the one pushing was {thief}, and on it were two wooden crates.

rumor.note: {boss} took the canned goods to sell, and altered the waybill to cover it
prose: !Some say it was {boss} who took the canned goods to sell, and who altered the waybill to cover it.
!There is another story, too, that {boss} sold the canned goods on the quiet.

detail.t: The back door of the freight house gives onto a lane with no lamp at night.

calm.t: Six cases of canned goods are not worth much. But everything in the freight house was ordered by somebody in town, and every case that goes missing is one household's order that never arrives.

neutral.t: Five cents a can is half the store price. Nobody who paid for the goods could make money at that price, unless the goods cost nothing.
What went missing from the waybill were canned peaches, and what is being sold at the market are canned peaches. The two match.

hot.t: Nobody wheels crates out a back door at midnight to make a delivery for the freight house.
Goods go missing from the freight house, and somebody sells the same goods at half price at the market.

any.t: Six cases at twenty-four cans a case comes to a hundred and forty-four cans. That is not something a person carries off in a coat pocket.
When one person suddenly has that many canned goods and is in a hurry to sell them at half price, the buyers ought to ask where they came from.
There were two crates on the handcart, and six cases are missing from the waybill. The other four have either gone already or have yet to go.
The crates were not opened, and whether they held canned goods is for the stationmaster to say. This paper writes only that it saw a handcart and two crates.

This paper has heard the story that {boss.short} took the goods. But it was {boss.short} who checked the waybill and reported the loss, and taking the goods only to go hunting for them makes little sense. This paper has found nothing to support the story.
The people who sleep rough behind the railway station have always walked past the freight house at night without anyone asking why.

{target.short} says what was on the handcart that night were {target.his} own belongings.

neutral.t: How the freight house back door is kept from now on is up to the stationmaster.

Fall is the time to lay in firewood, and families in town have begun hauling it home a cartload at a time.
The woods north of the sawmill are entered only by the mill's own felling crew, once a year, in spring.

stumps.note: thirty-odd new stumps appeared on the north side of the sawmill's woods this month
prose: thirty-odd new stumps have appeared on the north side of the sawmill's woods this month.
thirty-odd new stumps have appeared on the north side of the sawmill's woods this month, the cuts still white.

firewood.note: {cutter} delivers firewood door to door at a dollar a load, half the going price
prose: {cutter} delivers firewood door to door at a dollar a load, half the going price.
{cutter} has lately been driving a wagon round town delivering firewood at a dollar a load, half what it fetches elsewhere.

logs.note: {cutter} drove a wagon out of the woods in the middle of the night, loaded with logs
prose: #night#, {cutter} drove a wagon out of the woods loaded with logs.

prose.t: !#night#, at the edge of the woods, this paper's reporter saw {cutter} drive a wagon out from among the trees, stacked high with logs and roped down tight.
!This paper's reporter kept watch on the north side of the woods #night#, and heard sawing among the trees. Toward daybreak, {cutter} came out with a wagonload of logs.
!#night#, a wagon came along the dirt track at the edge of the woods carrying fresh-sawn logs. The driver was {cutter}, and this paper's reporter was standing by the road.

rumor.note: the foreman took money to let {cutter} into the woods
prose: !Some say the foreman took money to let {cutter} into the woods.
!Some also say the foreman was paid to let {cutter} into the woods.

detail.t: In town, firewood goes for two dollars a load.

calm.t: Every household burns wood in winter, and everyone is glad of cheap firewood. Those buying it may not know where it was cut.

neutral.t: A load of firewood for a dollar is half the going price. Only someone who never paid for the trees could sell it that cheap.
Thirty-odd trees are not felled in a night or two. Whoever cut them spent a good many days in those woods.

hot.t: The woods belong to the mill, and the firewood is sold by {cutter.short}. Whose pocket the money goes into is easy to work out.

any.t: One tree makes about a load of firewood. Thirty-odd stumps make thirty-odd loads, and at a dollar a load that comes to thirty-odd dollars.
Hauling logs out of the woods at night might be explained as laying in wood for one's own stove. But the firewood {cutter.short} has is sold door to door, not burned at home.
This paper cannot tell which trees that wagonload of logs came from. But the fresh stumps on the north side stand right beside the dirt track the logs went out on.
The story that the foreman took money to let someone into the woods, this paper has not been able to confirm. It is noted here and not taken as true.
Whoever cuts the trees makes a few dozen dollars over the winter, and next spring the sawmill has a few dozen fewer trees to fell. The men at the mill live off those woods too.
A farmer has no work in the fields in winter, and cutting and selling firewood is an honest trade. But the trees have to be one's own.

denied.t: {target.short} says the firewood is deadfall gathered along the riverbank.
{target.short} says the logs hauled that night came off {target.his} own land.

calm.t: When buying firewood this winter, it does no harm to ask where it was cut.

Cows give less milk in winter, and butter is never dearer than at this time of year.

rumor.note: {farmer} sold off one of the cows long ago
prose: !Some say {farmer} sold one of the cows long ago.
!Some also say {farmer} sold off one of the cows long ago.

detail.t: One cow gives roughly three pounds of butter a week.

calm.t: Those who eat the butter may not taste the lard in it. The store that sent it back did.

neutral.t: One cow gives about three pounds of butter a week, so two give six. The receiving book records twice that, and the extra half did not come from any cow.
The store sent the butter back twice, which means it was not a single slip.

hot.t: Lard costs far less than butter. Work a lump of lard into the butter, and it still sells at the butter price.

any.t: The lard being worked in is what this paper saw; the figures in the receiving book are what this paper found. One shows how it was done, the other how much.
The smell of lard on melting is what the buyers noticed; the lard worked in by the cold spring is what this paper saw. The nose and the eye tell the same story.

As for the story that {target.short} sold a cow long ago, this paper did not go and count the cows. Even with both cows in the barn, the butter in the receiving book is already double what they could give.
Lard in the butter will not make anyone ill. But the buyers paid for butter.
This paper knows it is not easy to keep a family on two cows. But the extra half came out of the pockets of the households buying the butter.

denied.t: {target.short} says the taste in the butter comes from the cows being out on new grass.
{target.short} says butter from other farms has been entered in the book under {target.his} name.

calm.t: When you bring butter home from the general store, it does no harm to melt a little first and smell it.

hot.t: Someone is fishing with dynamite, and the dynamite came out of the sawmill.
The fish in the Grey River were not netted. They were blown up.

scene.t: Before dawn the river bend is at its quietest; the only sound is the fishermen poling out to set their nets.
Once spring comes the fish run upstream, and the water in the bend is at its deepest.
In summer the river runs low, and the stretch at the bend is the only place left near town where a net can still be set.
Every spring the sawmill clears ground and blasts out the stumps with dynamite, and it keeps a few cases in its storeroom the year round.

deadfish.note: dead fish have washed up on the lower Grey River several times this month, all with their bellies burst
prose: dead fish have washed up on the lower Grey River several times this month, all with their bellies burst open.

when the sawmill storeroom was checked against its books, half a case of the dynamite used for blasting stumps was missing, and {keeper} is looking into it.

!It was not yet light. First came a spark out on the bend, then a bang. This paper's reporter saw {fisher} pole a boat out to collect the fish.

rumor.note: {keeper} sold the dynamite to {fisher} on the quiet
prose: !Some say {keeper} sold the dynamite to {fisher} on the quiet.
!There is another story, too, that {keeper} sold {fisher} the dynamite on the side.

detail.t: The dynamite used on stumps comes in charges no bigger than a man's palm, wrapped in oiled paper.

calm.t: The fishermen live off this river, and in other years their nets never took the small fry along with the rest.

neutral.t: A fish with a burst belly has had something go off in the water near it. A fish taken in a net comes up whole.
Blasting a stump does not take half a case of dynamite. Where the missing dynamite went, the books do not say.

hot.t: One blast and every fish in the bend, large and small, turns belly-up. What will be left in the river to catch next year?

any.t: Dead fish with burst bellies, and half a case of the sawmill's dynamite missing, both in the same month. This paper does not believe it is a coincidence.
What {fisher.short} threw in was a lit paper bundle. What was inside could not be made out from the bank, but what the sawmill is missing is dynamite wrapped in oiled paper.
Dynamite going off in the water can hurt anyone close by. That nobody else was on the bend before dawn was luck, not good practice.
For the story that {keeper.short} sold the dynamite on the quiet, this paper has found no evidence yet. Who holds the key to the storeroom, the sawmill knows best.
A fisherman knows better than anyone that it takes years for the fish in a bend to grow back.

denied.t: {target.short} says that morning on the bend was spent setting nets.
{target.short} says the fish were poisoned by waste water from the sawmill upstream.

neutral.t: It will be years before the fish come back to the bend.

coop.note: eleven chickens have gone from the henhouse of {victim} this month

Nobody who kills a chicken in the back yard needs to go down to the river to pluck it.

hot.t: Stealing from a family's henhouse is lower than stealing saw blades from the mill.

A laying hen gives five or six eggs a week. What was taken was not only the chickens but every egg they would have laid.
As for the talk that {victim.short} sold the birds, this paper has not been able to confirm it. It can only be counted as gossip.
Someone sleeping rough behind the railway station suddenly has dressed chickens to sell, and the tavern kitchen asks no questions.

denied.t: {target.short} says the chickens sold to the tavern were bought from a farm north of town.

!There is another story, too, that {buyer} paid {clerk} cash for the flour, at eighty cents a sack.

detail.t: Each family on relief draws one sack a month.

calm.t: Relief flour is what the state sends for the families hardest up. One sack is a month of biscuits and gravy for one household.

neutral.t: Forty in, twenty-five out: the books are fifteen sacks short. If those fifteen are still in the storeroom, one look will settle it.
The sacks say "Not for Sale" in plain print, and both the seller and the buyer can read.

hot.t: Flour given free to the poor, sitting on a shelf with a price on it.

any.t: The town hall is fifteen sacks of relief flour short, and the general store has flour on its shelves in sacks printed with the same words. The two ends meet.
Fifteen sacks missing from the books, and the person who keeps the books carrying flour out after dark. This paper need do no more than set the two side by side.
Relief flour can be carried in and out of the town hall in broad daylight. Whoever chose the back door after dark knew this was not town business.
As for eighty cents a sack, this paper has seen no money change hands, and that does not count.
The clerk keeps all the town's accounts, and the relief book is in the hands of {target.short} as well. What is missing from it, only {target.short} can explain.

denied.t: {target.short} says the other fifteen sacks are still in the storeroom and were simply never entered in the book.
{target.short} says the flour that night was lent to the general store to tide it over.

neutral.t: This paper will keep asking where those fifteen sacks went.

The relief flour passed through the hands of {clerk.full}.

detail.t: Banns must stay up for three Sundays, and only if no one in town objects may the wedding take place.

calm.t: A wedding is a happy day for two families, and at such a time this paper would rather hold its tongue.

neutral.t: There is nothing strange in a man having married before; there are widowers and divorced men enough. But what became of that first marriage, this paper does not yet know.
A letter signed "Your Wife" could be a joke, or an old flame. Once a month for this long, it does not look like an old flame.

hot.t: A family down south, and another about to be made in Greyriver: somebody, on one side or the other, is being deceived.

any.t: Banns are posted on the church door so that anyone who knows of an impediment may speak. This paper knows of one, and so speaks here.
The record says there was a wedding six years ago; the letters say that wife is writing still. Put the two together, and she has not gone anywhere.
Banns stay up three Sundays precisely so the town has time to speak.
As for two children down south, this paper has found no proof, and does not take it seriously.
When a newcomer marries someone from town, the town will naturally ask a few more questions.

denied.t: {target.short} says the marriage down south ended long ago, only the papers were never filed.
{target.short} says the letters are from {target.his} sister.

calm.t: Whether the wedding goes ahead is a matter for the two families. This paper has said what it had to say.

neutral: This paper has learned something concerning {user.full}, and it has to do with medicine.

neutral.t: {user.full} has nodded off in company more than once lately. This paper looked into why.

hot.t: {user.full} has been keeping a secret, and the clinic's books have been keeping it too.
Someone who cannot put down the bottle is still making decisions for this town.

scene.t: The clinic's medicine cabinet has two shelves, and the laudanum is kept on the top one, under lock.
Those who run the town's affairs see a great many people in a day, and a single sitting can take up a whole afternoon.
Once a week the hired girls clear out their employers' rubbish, and nobody knows better what a house throws away.

prose: {user} has had a bottle of laudanum filled at the clinic every week for a year without a break.

prose.t: !This paper went through the clinic's dispensing book: the name of {user} appears once every week, always for laudanum, from this time last year until now.
!This paper found at the clinic that {user} has had a bottle of laudanum made up every week for a year, without missing once.

vials.note: {maid} carries four or five empty brown medicine bottles a month out of the house of {user}
prose: {maid} carries four or five empty medicine bottles a month out of the house of {user}, all of them small and brown.
four or five small brown medicine bottles a month go out with the rubbish from the house of {user}, and it is {maid} who carries them out.

doze.note: {user} has twice this month fallen asleep sitting up in broad daylight, and woke only after being called several times
prose: {user} has twice this month fallen asleep sitting up in broad daylight, and had to be called several times before waking.
twice this month {user} dozed off sitting up in the middle of the day, and did not wake until those nearby had called out several times.

rumor.note: {user} buys the medicine on the black market in the city
prose: !Some say {user} buys the stuff on the black market in the city.
!There is another story, too, that {user} gets the medicine from the black market in the city.

detail.t: The proper dose of laudanum is a few drops at a time.

calm.t: Dozing off in the daytime may mean no more than a bad night's sleep, and this paper makes no more of it than that.

neutral.t: Laudanum is a medicine for pain, and a little goes a long way. Used as the doctor directs, one week's bottle would last a person for months.
Small brown bottles like these most likely came from the clinic.

hot.t: A bottle of laudanum a week, asleep in a chair in broad daylight, and the town's business left in such hands.

any.t: The clinic fills a bottle every week; the house of {user.short} throws out four or five empties a month. Every bottle that goes in is drunk to the bottom.
Dozing off in daylight, taken alone, could be tiredness. But the clinic records a bottle of laudanum for {target.him} every week, and that is more than tiredness.
Laudanum prescribed by a doctor is no crime. What this paper asks is this: what illness is it that has not let up for a single week in a year?

It is said the medicine comes from the black market, but what this paper found is the clinic's own record, and the medicine there is the genuine article. The black-market story this paper does not credit.
The one who stands in the pulpit each Sunday goes to the clinic each week for a bottle of medicine.
The mayor sees a great many people in a day. Fall asleep in front of them once, and the whole town knows.
The entries in the town register are in the hand of {target.short}. With a bottle of laudanum a week, is that hand still steady?
When a teacher dozes off in class, the children are the first to notice.

denied.t: {target.short} says it is a painkiller the doctor prescribed for an old injury.
{target.short} says {target.he} had simply slept badly those nights.

declined: {target.short} says what medicine {target.he} takes is {target.his} own affair.

calm.t: This paper hopes {target.short} will go and see the doctor about it.

This paper has a few things to say about what happened on the day of the drawing.

hot.t: The ten-cent raffle ticket you bought never had a chance of winning.
First prize was a radio, but no radio ever came to Greyriver.

scene.t: In this town only the mayor's house and the tavern have a radio, and on Saturday nights the tavern is packed with people listening to the broadcasts.
The tavern was packed the afternoon the raffle was drawn, with people crowded into the doorway.
Winter nights are long and the town has little to amuse it; a raffle ticket can give a person something to look forward to for weeks.

prose: {organizer} is selling raffle tickets at ten cents apiece, with a radio for first prize.
{organizer} has lately been going about town selling raffle tickets, ten cents each, and says first prize is a radio.

noradio.note: the post office parcel book shows no radio delivered to town in months
prose: the post office parcel book shows that no radio has come to town in months.

prose.t: !This paper went through the post office parcel book for the past several months. Every parcel, large and small, is entered there, and not one of them is a radio.
!This paper read the post office parcel book page by page: from the day the tickets went on sale, not one parcel delivered to town has been a radio.

rigged.note: on drawing day the number {organizer} pulled from the hat had been hidden up a sleeve, and the winner was {winner}
prose: on the day of the drawing, the number {organizer} pulled from the hat had been hidden up a sleeve beforehand, and the winner was {winner}.

prose.t: !When the raffle was drawn, this paper's reporter was standing by the tavern counter. {organizer} reached into the hat, and the number that came out had slipped down from a sleeve. The winner was {winner}.

!At the drawing, this paper's reporter stood only a few steps from {organizer} and saw it plainly: the number was not drawn from the hat but had been tucked up a sleeve all along. The name read out was {winner}.
!At the drawing, the hand of {organizer} paused inside the hat. From close by, this paper's reporter saw a slip of card slide from the cuff into the palm. The winner was {winner}.

rumor.note: {winner} is a cousin of {organizer}
prose: !Some say {winner} is a cousin of {organizer}.
!Some also say that {winner} and {organizer} are cousins.

detail.t: The raffle numbers were written on slips of card, all the same size and the same color.

calm.t: Ten cents a ticket: anyone could afford one, and so nearly everyone bought one.

neutral.t: At ten cents a ticket, it would take several hundred tickets to pay for a radio.
If there were really a first prize, it would have to be shipped from somewhere. The post office parcel book has no record of it.

hot.t: A raffle is supposed to be a game of luck. With the number up a sleeve, the only thing being drawn is the ticket buyers' money.

any.t: The tickets were sold and the money taken in, but no first prize ever came through the post office. Where the ticket money went ought to be accounted for.
If the winner was settled beforehand, there was never any need for the radio to come at all.
A raffle is drawn in public precisely so everyone can see there is nothing in the drawer's hand.
As for the winner being a cousin of {organizer.short}, this paper found no tie between the two families. It is set down here only as talk.
The tavern keeper ran the raffle, and most of the ticket buyers are regulars at the tavern.
Raffle tickets were sold over the general store counter, and people buying flour picked one up while they were at it.

denied.t: {target.short} says the radio is being shipped straight from the city and does not go through the post office.
{target.short} says the number was drawn from the hat in front of everyone.

neutral.t: Anyone still holding a raffle ticket would do well to keep it. It is a receipt for ten cents.
